analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC enforce antitrust law against tax-exempt hospital systems.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee after a single subcommittee referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Nonprofit hospitals are largely exempt from Federal Trade Commission antitrust enforcement because the FTC's power covers for-profit corporations. This bill would change the FTC's legal definition of "corporation" so that tax-exempt hospitals and hospital cooperatives could be investigated and challenged for anticompetitive mergers or conduct. The bill was introduced in April 2023, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and received no further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and communities served by hospital systems: FTC oversight of tax-exempt hospitals could block or unwind anticompetitive hospital mergers and pricing practices, which research links to higher prices without quality gains. Taxpayers and employers who ultimately foot hospital bills through insurance, Medicare, and self-funded plans would also benefit if consolidation-driven price increases were checked.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying hospital bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the definition of "corporation" in Section 4 of the FTC Act to include hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations that are tax-exempt under section 501(c)(3), placing them within the FTC's enforcement reach [S3].

Hospital systems across much of the country are tax-exempt nonprofits, and the FTC currently lacks general antitrust jurisdiction over them, so this change would make FTC merger review and enforcement available against the sector [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large tax-exempt hospital systems and hospital cooperatives, which would face FTC merger scrutiny and potential enforcement actions, including possible litigation costs, blocked deals, or divestitures. Hospital trade groups would likely argue the change creates legal uncertainty for mission-driven institutions operating on thin margins.

drawbacks.text: The bill is extremely narrow: a two-word amendment to one statutory definition with no additional funding, staffing, or study of how the FTC would handle the new jurisdiction, leaving enforcement capacity an open question [S3].

Defenders of nonprofit hospitals argue that rural and safety-net hospitals operate on thin margins and that broad antitrust exposure could deter the mergers and affiliations some struggling community hospitals need to survive, potentially reducing local access to care.
Even with FTC jurisdiction, challenging completed hospital mergers after the fact is slow and often unsuccessful, so the bill alone would not quickly undo existing consolidation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy idea is well-targeted: hospital consolidation is a leading driver of rising health care prices, and nonprofits now dominate the industry while sitting outside FTC jurisdiction. But the bill is a minimal, one-sentence fix with no added enforcement resources, and it never advanced, so its real-world benefit was zero. The honest weighing is that the concept has merit while the bill, as introduced and left to die, accomplished nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the Combatting Hospital Monopolies Act on April 25, 2023 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
On April 28, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, and no further action was recorded before the 118th Congress ended [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a House Democrat, and never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large tax-exempt hospital systems, which remain outside FTC antitrust enforcement and free to merge and consolidate without federal competition review. Patients gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor; no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is visible, and the committee simply never acted.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt hospital systems and hospital cooperatives
industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from FTC antitrust enforcement, exposing their mergers and contracts to federal competition review. Hospital consolidation has raised prices for patients and insurers, so the industry's interest in staying exempt runs against the public's interest in lower prices.
The FTC would gain enforcement jurisdiction over a major sector of the hospital market, expanding its ability to police consolidation that raises consumer prices.
